blocks.text: Data visualisation presents data clearly, so patterns, trends and relationships can be seen before statistical tests are applied. Visuals make complex data easier to interpret, reduce misunderstandings, make differences between groups easy to compare, and help find outliers and anomalies (Fig 7.2). They give visual evidence that supports better decisions.

Visualisation turns raw data into meaningful visual forms, helping researchers understand large datasets that are hard to analyse as numbers. It highlights trends, distributions and variation, makes results easier to explain to technical and non-technical audiences, and reduces errors by making unusual patterns visible.

blocks.long_description: Each chart answers a different question: how groups compare, how things change, or how two variables move together.

blocks.text: Visuals link results directly to the hypothesis, letting researchers see whether the data supports it or not. A comparison chart can show the difference between control and treatment groups, a line graph can confirm a predicted trend, and a scatter plot can show a relationship stated in the hypothesis. Visual evidence strengthens the reasoning, though the decision itself still comes from the statistical test.

blocks.prompt: Which chart would best show whether the treatment group's average marks were higher than the control group's, and why should a test still be done?
blocks.explanation: A bar chart of the two group means. The chart shows a difference, but only a hypothesis test shows whether the difference is larger than chance would produce.

items: Visualisation shows patterns, differences and outliers before and after testing.
Bar: compare groups; line: trends; pie: proportions; scatter: relationships.
Visuals support the hypothesis decision but do not replace the test.
